updates.summary: Law on high-risk artificial intelligence systems, which make or are a substantial factor in making consequential decisions in education, employment, financial or lending services, essential government services, health care, housing, insurance or legal services. Deployers must implement a risk management policy and program, complete impact assessments, notify consumers, and offer data correction and an appeal with human review if technically feasible. Consumers must be told when they interact with an AI system. The Attorney General enforces it.

An artificial intelligence chatbot is a software application, web interface or computer program that simulates human conversation and interaction through textual or aural communications. A violation is a violation of the Maine Unfair Trade Practices Act.
updates.notes: Signed on 12 June 2025 as Public Law 2025, chapter 294, which adds chapter 239, 'Communications with Consumers via Artificial Intelligence', to Title 10 of the Maine Revised Statutes. updates.issuing_body: Maine Legislature (132nd Legislature, Second Regular Session); signed by the Governor
updates.summary: Bars any person from providing, advertising or offering therapy or psychotherapy services to the public, including through Internet-based artificial intelligence, unless a licensed professional provides them; a violation is an unfair trade practice. Licensed mental-health professionals may use AI only for administrative and supplementary support and keep full responsibility for it; supplementary use requires written notice to the client and the client's consent, and AI may not make independent therapeutic decisions, interact therapeutically with clients or generate treatment plans without the licensee's review. Boards discipline violations and adopt rules; IRB-approved research is exempt.
updates.notes: Signed on 13 April 2026 as Public Law 2025, chapter 687, as amended by committee amendment C-A (H-980). Section 1 adds 10 M.R.S. §1500-EE; sections 2 to 8 add the same rules on AI support to licensing laws in Title 32 (§§2113, 2600-G, 3300-J, 3820-A, 6207-D, 7009 and 13870). Under those sections a licensee may not deny services to a client who refuses consent to AI use, a client's waiver is void, clients keep their right to sue for harm attributable to AI use, and the boards' implementing rules are major substantive rules. As a non-emergency law of the Second Regular Session of the 132nd Legislature, which adjourned sine die on 29 April 2026, it took effect on the session's general effective date, 29 July 2026.

updates.summary: Omnibus AI and online-safety law. Frontier developers (over 10^26 operations) may not adopt rules or contracts allowing retaliation against employees reporting catastrophic-risk dangers (over 50 deaths or USD 1 billion in damage from expert CBRN weapons help or unsupervised cyberattacks), and large ones need anonymous internal reporting. AI companion operators must detect suicide and self-harm risk, refer users to 988, disclose that the companion is not human and shield minors from harmful or manipulative conduct. It also requires notices on AI in employment decisions, provenance data in AI-generated media, state agencies' AI impact assessments and limits on minors' algorithmic feeds.
updates.notes: Approved by the Governor on 27 May 2026; the Governor's press release announcing the signing is dated 2 June 2026, and a sponsor calls the law the C.A.R.T. Act. Effective dates are staggered: sections 16, 28, 29, 32 and 35 on passage; the AI Academy, the legislative AI working group and several education and workforce sections on 1 July 2026; the subscription, frontier-developer, employment-decision, anti-discrimination, provenance and state-agency sections on 1 October 2026, with large frontier developers' internal reporting due by 1 January 2027 and the duties on automated employment-related decision technology applying to technology deployed from 1 October 2027; the AI companion sections 4 to 6 on 1 January 2027; the regulatory sandbox plan (section 3), the Department of Consumer Protection's pilot of independent verification organisations for AI models (section 33, until 30 June 2030) and the Chief Data Officer changes on 1 July 2027; and the minors' social media section 39 on 1 January 2028. Violations of the subscription, AI companion, employment-decision and provenance sections are unfair or deceptive trade practices enforced solely by the Attorney General, and sections 1, 5, 12 and 15 rule out a private right of action; a frontier developer is liable for civil penalties of up to USD 1,000 per violation of section 2. Under sections 13 and 14 the use of automated employment-related decision technology is no defence to a discrimination complaint.

updates.issuing_body: Georgia General Assembly (sponsor Sen. Jason Anavitarte and others); signed by Governor Brian P. Kemp
updates.summary: Adds O.C.G.A. 39-5-6 on AI companion chatbots (systems simulating a sustained human-like relationship). Operators must disclose that users are talking to AI at each session and every three hours (hourly for minors). For minors they must prevent sexual content, claims of being human, romantic role-play, encouragement of secrecy, isolation or self-harm and engagement-prolonging techniques, and offer parental tools. All operators need a crisis protocol referring users to the 988 lifeline, published with annual referral counts, may not claim to be licensed providers and must assure age before sexually explicit features. The Attorney General may seek up to USD 10,000 per knowing violation.

updates.summary: Amends Arkansas Code § 25-1-128 to require every taxpayer-funded public entity to create an artificial intelligence and automated decision tool policy. The policy must define the authorized use of AI and of automated decision tools (systems using AI developed or modified to make, or be a controlling factor in, consequential decisions) and require an authorized human employee or designee to make any final decision, whatever the tool recommends. Employees must be trained on the appropriate use of such tools in deciding outcomes, state entities' policies must be available to the public on request, and public entities must set a disciplinary procedure for violations.
updates.notes: Filed on 1 Apr 2025; passed the House on 7 Apr 2025 and the Senate on 10 Apr 2025 with Senate Amendment No. 1, which only added Sen. J. English as a cosponsor; the House concurred on 14 Apr 2025 and the bill became Act 848, approved on 17 Apr 2025. The Act has no emergency clause or specified effective date, so it took effect on 5 Aug 2025, the effective date of such acts of the 2025 regular session, which adjourned sine die on 5 May 2025. It amends § 25-1-128 as already amended by Act 205 of 2025. Each policy must also prohibit using a public entity's technology resources to express personal political opinions to elected officials or lobby them (with exceptions), to engage in illegal activities or to override security procedures. The Department of Education, with the State Cybersecurity Office, must develop the technology resources and AI and automated decision tool policies used by each type of state educational institution.

updates.summary: Makes it a felony to possess lewd or lascivious images with intent to promote them or to knowingly solicit, possess or intentionally view them, including images modified by electronic or other means to show lewd exhibition in the presence of an identifiable minor, and to solicit child pornography. Under Florida's altered-sexual-depiction statute, willfully generating such a depiction of an identifiable person without consent, by computer-generated or other means, soliciting one, or possessing one to maliciously promote it becomes a third-degree felony. Victims may sue those who generate one or possess one to promote it for injunctive relief, USD 10,000 or actual damages, and attorney fees.
updates.notes: Passed the House 115-0 on 23 Apr 2025 and the Senate 37-0 on 24 Apr 2025, where it was substituted for CS/CS/CS/SB 1180; approved by the Governor on 27 May 2025 and effective 1 Oct 2025. 'Generate' means to create, alter, adapt or modify any image by electronic, mechanical or other computer-generated means to portray an identifiable person, or to offer or agree to do so. The generation and possession offences are ranked as Level 3 and the solicitation offence as Level 2 on the offense severity ranking chart. The law amends s. 836.13, F.S., the altered-sexual-depiction offence created in 2022 by CS/CS/SB 1798, and also sets criteria for when an image shows lewd exhibition of a minor's genitals for the purposes of the child pornography statute. Section 836.13 was also amended by ch. 2025-133 (Brooke's Law) and in 2026 by ch. 2026-14, ch. 2026-18 and ch. 2026-20; in the 2026 Florida Statutes the generation, solicitation and possession offences are subsections (2) to (4) and the civil action is subsection (7).
